title: Centering prayer
hook: Thomas Keating and other monks taught a silent prayer with one sacred word

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of the Cross and a dark night, when prayer goes flat and something quieter grows. Your line was a dark night. Did something feel flat, and did you do it anyway, gently? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

Monks in a Massachusetts abbey kept meeting young visitors who were hungry for meditation. Some had found it on other paths. The story told about the beginning of centering prayer is that the abbot, Thomas Keating, wondered aloud whether his own Christian tradition had a quiet practice like that, one that could be taught simply, to anyone, outside a monastery. His fellow monks went looking. One of them, William Meninger, found an answer on a shelf, in a book this week has already opened: The Cloud of Unknowing, with its one short word. Out of that search came a way of praying with almost nothing in it. Today's word is the name they gave it.
screen: `YOUNG VISITORS, HUNGRY FOR SILENCE.` → `DOES OUR OWN TRADITION HAVE ONE?` → `AN ANSWER ON A SHELF.`

segments.voice: Centering prayer looks simple, and its teachers say it is. Here it is in four turns. First, the door Jesus names. Keating pointed to a line from the Sermon on the Mount: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." The closet there is an inner room. Centering prayer treats it as an inner room in the person. Second, the sacred word. You choose one short word, like God, or peace, or love. The surprise is what the word is for. It isn't a magic sound, and it isn't meant to be repeated constantly like a mantra or the Jesus Prayer. In Keating's teaching, it's a sign of intention: a way of saying, I consent to God's presence and action within me. Third, thoughts. Thoughts will come, and in this prayer that's no failure. Keating used to compare them to boats going by on a river. You don't chase them and you don't fight them. When you notice you've climbed aboard one, you return, ever so gently, to the sacred word. Then you let even the word fade. Fourth, consent. That's the heart of it. Centering prayer doesn't try to produce a feeling, a vision, or a calm mind. It's an act of saying yes, again and again, without words. Keating taught that the fruit shows up later, in ordinary life, not during the prayer itself. Some practice it with a group, and Keating suggested a longer sit than today's, twice a day. But the shape is the same at any length: a word, a yes, and a lot of gentle returning.
screen: `ENTER INTO THY CLOSET.` · `ONE SACRED WORD, AS A SIGN.` · `THOUGHTS ARE BOATS ON A RIVER.` · `THE HEART OF IT: CONSENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one word. Choose it now, a short one. If you pray, a word like God or peace. If not, a word like yes, or open. Close your eyes and let it settle, quietly, once. Then sit. When you notice you've drifted off on a thought, a plan, a memory, even a good insight, don't scold yourself. Just come back, gently, to the word, and let it go again. The returning is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Centering prayer. A silent Christian prayer with one sacred word, used as a sign of consent, and returned to gently whenever thoughts carry you off. Today's word.
Your line: consent. Today, when something arrives you didn't plan, a delay, a change, a person, try one quiet yes before you decide what to do about it. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: People who practice centering prayer sit in silence with eyes closed, gently returning to a chosen sacred word when they notice thoughts, sometimes in groups that meet in churches and retreat houses.

Origin story (Keating as abbot, young people seeking meditation, William Meninger finding The Cloud of Unknowing) is told as 'the story told about the beginning'; the abbey is described only as 'a Massachusetts abbey' (St. Joseph's Abbey, Spencer). Basil Pennington, also central, is not named for length. No dates given.
